item.title: What is the difference between a major and a minor?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: A major is your primary field of academic study, requiring a significant number of specialized courses and accounting for a large portion of your degree requirements. A minor is an optional, secondary concentration of study that requires fewer credit hours (typically 15-18 credits) and allows you to explore an additional area of interest.

item.title: How many credit hours do I need to take each semester to be considered a full-time student?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: To maintain full-time undergraduate student status, you must enroll in a minimum of 12 credit hours per semester. However, to complete a standard 120-credit bachelor's degree program in four years, students typically need to average 15 credit hours per semester (usually 4 or 5 courses).

item.title: What are general education or core curriculum requirements?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: General education requirements are a foundational suite of mandatory courses outside of your specific major. They span foundational subject categories—such as natural sciences, humanities, mathematics, social sciences, and analytical writing—designed to give all university graduates a well-rounded academic background.

item.title: Can I switch my major after starting a program, and how does that process work?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Yes, most programs permit students to change their major. The process involves meeting with an Academic Advisor to evaluate how your completed credits transfer into the new program framework, filling out a Change of Major declaration form, and obtaining authorization from the relevant department head.

item.title: What is the role of an Academic Advisor?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Academic Advisors guide you through your educational journey. They help you understand degree track workflows, select and plan your semester course schedules, ensure you meet pre-requisite tracks, monitor your progress toward graduation milestones, and connect you with university resources if you encounter academic challenges.

item.title: What is a prerequisite course?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: A prerequisite is a specific foundational course or milestone that you must successfully complete with a passing grade before you are permitted to register for a more advanced, higher-level course in that subject sequence.

item.title: How do I apply for an independent study or research project with a faculty member?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Students must identify a faculty member whose research field aligns with their interests, present a formal or informal study proposal, and request their mentorship. If accepted, you must complete an Independent Study Authorization form with the department coordinator to receive course credit hours.

item.title: What academic support resources are available if I am struggling with a course?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: The university provides comprehensive free support, including centralized Peer Tutoring Centers, Writing Labs for essay guidance, Math Clinics, and professor office hours. Students are strongly encouraged to utilize these free resources as early in the academic term as possible.

item.title: What does it mean if a course is listed as hybrid?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: A hybrid or blended course combines traditional in-person classroom instruction with structured online components. For example, a hybrid class might meet on-campus once a week for interactive laboratory modules or discussions, while completing asynchronous lectures and assignments via the university's online learning portal.

item.title: What is an internship course, and can I earn credit toward my degree for work experience?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: An internship course allows you to earn academic credit hours while gaining professional experience in a career field related to your major. These courses require department pre-approval, are supervised by a faculty adviser, and require specific academic deliverables such as journals or a final summary paper.

item.title: What is Academic Probation, and how can a student clear their record?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Academic Probation occurs when a student's cumulative grade point average (GPA) falls below the university's minimum requirement threshold (typically a 2.0). To clear probation status, the student must work with an advisor to follow an academic success plan and raise their cumulative GPA back above the threshold within a designated number of credit hours.

item.title: How do I apply to study abroad without delaying my graduation timeline?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: You should coordinate early with the Study Abroad Office and your Academic Advisor to select an international partner institution that offers pre-approved equivalent courses. Ensuring that the credits you earn abroad directly fulfill your core program or major requirements will keep you on track for your scheduled graduation date.

item.title: What is the difference between an asynchronous online course and a synchronous online course?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Synchronous online courses require you to log in at specific, scheduled times to attend live, real-time lectures and interact with classmates. Asynchronous online courses do not have set meeting times, allowing you to watch pre-recorded lectures and complete assignments on your own schedule, provided you meet the weekly course deadlines.

item.title: What are the requirements to graduate with honors or Latin honors?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Graduating with honors typically requires achieving an exceptional cumulative GPA threshold calculated at completion. For example, Cum Laude often requires a 3.50–3.69 GPA, Magna Cum Laude requires a 3.70–3.89 GPA, and Summa Cum Laude requires a 3.90 or higher, alongside any specific departmental thesis mandates.

item.title: How can I check my progress toward satisfying all my graduation requirements?
item.dc:creator: teampedal
item.content:encoded: Students can track their graduation track anytime by logging into the student portal and generating an automated Degree Audit report. This tool evaluates your completed and in-progress courses against your official catalog requirements, highlighting exactly which modules remain unfulfilled.

item.dc:creator: teampedal

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value:
The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science program offers an intensive, forward-thinking curriculum designed to explore the boundary between theoretical logic and real-world application. Students delve deep into computational systems, algorithmic thinking, software architectures, and automated technologies.

Rather than merely learning how to write code, computer science majors learn how to solve complex computational problems, design secure networks, optimize data processing systems, and train advanced machine learning models. Through engineering design laboratories, collaborative software projects, and algorithmic analysis, students gain a deep conceptual mastery of the hardware-software interface and code foundations that power today's global digital landscape.

Eligibility

To maintain the high academic standards of the College of Engineering and Computer Science, admission to the B.S.C.S. program is competitive and evaluates several metrics of academic performance.

  • Secondary School Education: Successful completion of a high school diploma or recognized equivalent curriculum.

  • Mathematics Foundations: A strong background in mathematics is vital for success in this program. Applicants are highly encouraged to have successfully completed pre-calculus or calculus.

  • Standardized Testing (Optional/Varies): Satisfactory SAT or ACT performance thresholds, with strong preference demonstrated toward quantitative reasoning or mathematical sections.

  • Technical Aptitude: While prior programming knowledge is beneficial, it is not strictly required. However, applicants should demonstrate strong analytical problem-solving skills, critical thinking, and logical reasoning capabilities.

  • Transfer Requirements: Transfer students looking to bridge into the program must present a cumulative GPA minimum (typically a 3.0 on a 4.0 scale) in core engineering or mathematics coursework.

Next Steps

If you are ready to begin your journey toward a dynamic career in technology, follow these sequential milestones to secure your enrollment:

  1. Schedule a Consultation: Connect with our Academic Advisors within the Department of Computer Science to map out your long-term academic degree tracker and evaluate credit transfers.

  2. Review the Course Catalog: Familiarize yourself with the upcoming introductory sequences—such as CS-103: Introduction to Programming and CS-201: Data Structures—to gauge semester weights.

  3. Submit Your Formal Application: Gather your official transcripts, standardized test reports, and an analytical statement of purpose detailing your academic ambitions, then apply through the online student portal.

  4. Explore Financial Aid and Scholarships: Review the university financial assistance programs, department-specific grants, and work-study research paths.

  5. Attend Orientation and Register: Once accepted, attend the engineering cohort orientation to meet faculty members, tour the campus tech spaces, and finalize your initial semester course schedule.

The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science requires the completion of 120 credit hours of coursework distributed across four key categories: General Education Core, Mathematics & Basic Sciences, Computer Science Core, and Advanced Technical Electives. The program is systematically structured to transition students from fundamental syntax to complex architectural design.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   B.S. IN COMPUTER SCIENCE (120 CR)                 |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Gen Ed Core   |  Math & Science  |   CS Core    |  Tech Electives  |
|    (30 CR)     |     (30 CR)      |   (45 CR)    |     (15 CR)      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+

Milestone Progression Track

Lower-Division Foundation (Freshman & Sophomore Years)

The first two years prioritize structural logic, programmatic syntax, and continuous mathematical frameworks. Students build computational thinking paradigms before moving into hardware-software boundaries.

  • Year 1: Algorithmic Foundations Students begin with CS-103: Introduction to Programming, learning syntax mechanics, variable scope, control flow, and functional decomposition. This runs parallel to MATH-101: Calculus I to reinforce limits and continuous optimization logic. The semester transitions into object-oriented concepts, basic algorithm construction, and a broader analysis of CS-118: Computing and Society, evaluating the ethical and social landscapes of computing technology.

  • Year 2: Data Structures & System Architecture Focus shifts to memory management and efficiency profiling. In CS-201: Data Structures, students implement, analyze, and optimize fundamental configurations like linked lists, hash tables, trees, and graphs. Simultaneously, CS-216: Computer Architecture deconstructs the hardware layer, exposing instruction set architectures (ISAs), assembly language, pipeline registers, and the direct interface between logic gates and running code. Advanced mathematics tracks (MATH-216: Linear Algebra and Calculus III) are integrated to prepare students for algorithmic scaling.

Upper-Division Mastery (Junior & Senior Years)

The final two years transition away from pure coding mechanics into systems-level implementation, abstract theoretical analysis, and project engineering.

  • Year 3: Systems & Software Engineering Students tackle concurrent operations and industrial workflows. CS-316: Operating Systems explores the core principles of process synchronization, thread scheduling, virtual memory allocation, and file systems. Concurrently, CS-301: Software Engineering operates as an experiential laboratory where student cohorts employ Agile methodologies, continuous integration pipelines (CI/CD), and software design patterns to build complex, full-scale software systems from the ground up.

  • Year 4: Theory, Specialization & Capstone The final year balances rigorous abstraction with practical application. Students dive into CS-401: Compiler Design to analyze lexical processing, abstract syntax trees, and code generation, while choosing from advanced specialization paths (e.g., Deep Learning, Cryptography, or Quantum Computing). The degree culminates in a multi-semester Senior Capstone Project, where teams engineer a production-ready solution to an industrial or research-grade computational problem, defending their architecture before a faculty panel.

A degree in Computer Science is incredibly versatile, yielding career opportunities that span nearly every modern sector, from finance and healthcare to specialized tech enterprises. Graduates enter the workforce highly equipped to assume roles such as:

  • Software Engineer / Full-Stack Developer: Designing, implementing, and optimizing large-scale software solutions, mobile platforms, or web applications.

  • Data Scientist / Machine Learning Engineer: Extracting actionable insights from complex empirical datasets and implementing predictive deep learning architectures.

  • Systems Architect / Network Engineer: Structural provisioning of secure, fault-tolerant network topologies and computing infrastructure for cloud operations.

  • Cybersecurity Analyst: Assessing software threat vectors, designing cryptographic defenses, and managing corporate internal control vulnerabilities.

Financial Aid & Program-Specific Funding

We believe financial constraints should never act as a barrier to technological innovation. Modern University offers a comprehensive web of financial assistance frameworks—combining gift aid, earned aid, and low-interest loans—to significantly reduce out-of-pocket costs for computer science majors.

Institutional & Departmental Scholarships

Scholarships represent merit-based gift aid that does not require repayment. The Department of Computer Science hosts several exclusive donor-funded scholarships tailored specifically to computing cohorts:

  • The Turing Innovation Award: A merit-based scholarship awarding up to $5,000 annually to incoming freshmen who demonstrate exceptional quantitative aptitude via mathematics placements or secondary school programming achievements.

  • Women in Technology (WIT) Endowed Scholarship: Designed to support and diversify the engineering pipeline, this fund provides $3,500 per year to outstanding female-identifying or non-binary students pursuing upper-division computer science tracks.

  • Tech Tower Capstone Grant: A merit stipend of $1,500 awarded to select senior student cohorts to fund physical prototyping, cloud infrastructure scaling, or hardware arrays required for their CS-499: Senior Capstone Project.

Need-Based Grants

Grants are primarily awarded based on demonstrated financial need derived from the student's financial profile:

  • Federal Pell Grants: Eligible undergraduate students can receive federal funding which scales dynamically depending on need.

  • College of Engineering Access Grant: A dedicated institutional fund that bridges the gap for computing majors whose family contribution tiers fall below baseline tuition requirements. This grant can cover up to 60% of the technical laboratory fees and required software costs.

Federal and Alternative Student Loans

When scholarships and grants do not fully cover the total cost of attendance, self-help loan options provide structured, low-interest borrowing alternatives:

  • Direct Subsidized Loans: Available to undergraduate students with demonstrated financial need. The federal government covers the accruing interest on these loans while the student is enrolled at least half-time, protecting them from compounding debt during their studies.

  • Direct Unsubsidized Loans: Available to all enrolled students regardless of financial need. Interest begins accumulating immediately upon disbursement, though principal repayment is deferred until six months post-graduation.

Earned Assistance: Undergraduate Research & Lab Assistantships

Upper-division computer science majors (Juniors and Seniors) can offset their educational costs while building highly relevant career resumes by applying for departmental employment. Lab Managers frequently hire qualified students as paid Peer Tutors or Laboratory Assistants for introductory sequences like CS-103, offering competitive hourly compensation or direct tuition credits.

Rather than merely learning how to balance books, accounting majors learn how to interpret complex financial data, evaluate corporate tax implications, design robust internal control systems, and provide the quantitative foundation required for high-level management and investment strategies. Through case-based seminars, professional accounting laboratories, and intensive regulatory analysis, students gain a deep conceptual mastery of the economic systems and ethical principles that power today’s global marketplace.

Eligibility

To maintain the high academic standards of the School of Business, admission to the B.S. in Accounting program is competitive and evaluates several metrics of academic performance.

  • Standardized Testing (Optional/Varies): Satisfactory SAT or ACT performance thresholds, with preference demonstrated toward quantitative reasoning or analytical sections.

  • Analytical Aptitude: While prior business experience is beneficial, it is not strictly required. However, applicants should demonstrate strong attention to detail, high ethical integrity, and critical thinking capabilities.

  • Transfer Requirements: Transfer students must present a cumulative GPA minimum (typically a 3.0 on a 4.0 scale) in core business or prerequisite mathematics coursework.

Milestone Progression Track

Lower-Division Foundation (Freshman & Sophomore Years)

The first two years prioritize accounting cycles, regulatory compliance, and foundational economic frameworks. Students build business intelligence paradigms before moving into advanced technical reporting.

  • Year 1: Financial & Managerial Foundations Students begin with ACC-101: Principles of Financial Accounting, learning the accounting equation, journal entries, ledger maintenance, and the preparation of core financial statements. This runs parallel to ECON-101: Principles of Economics to reinforce market behavior and resource allocation logic. The semester transitions into ACC-102: Managerial Accounting, where students evaluate cost-volume-profit relationships, budgeting, and performance measurement for internal decision-making.

  • Year 2: Intermediate Reporting & Business Law Focus shifts to GAAP standards and the legal environment of commerce. In ACC-201/202: Intermediate Accounting I & II, students perform deep dives into revenue recognition, asset valuation, and liability assessment. Simultaneously, BUS-210: Business Law & Ethics deconstructs the legal landscape governing contracts, agency, and the professional responsibilities inherent in fiduciary roles. Quantitative tracks (STAT-201: Business Statistics) are integrated to prepare students for data-driven financial forecasting.

Upper-Division Mastery (Junior & Senior Years)

The final two years transition away from procedural mechanics into complex tax strategy, audit methodologies, and enterprise-level financial governance.

  • Year 3: Taxation & Audit Systems Students tackle regulatory compliance and internal validation workflows. ACC-301: Federal Income Taxation explores the principles of tax law, entity-level planning, and the intersection of individual and corporate tax obligations. Concurrently, ACC-305: Auditing & Assurance Services operates as an experiential laboratory where student cohorts employ risk assessment frameworks, internal control evaluation, and evidence-gathering techniques to ensure financial statement accuracy and identify potential fraud.

  • Year 4: Theory, Specialization & Capstone The final year balances rigorous theoretical analysis with high-level professional application. Students dive into ACC-401: Advanced Accounting to analyze business combinations, consolidated financial statements, and foreign currency translations, while choosing from advanced specialization paths (e.g., Forensic Accounting, Data Analytics for Finance, or International Tax). The degree culminates in the Senior Capstone: Strategic Financial Management, where teams design a comprehensive business and tax strategy for a simulated corporate entity, defending their financial disclosures and strategic recommendations before a faculty and industry panel.
